subtitle: "Class 8 · Theme 5"

::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Generate random steps and look inside a stratum; fit an SSF; add
movement terms for a full iSSA; update and interpret the movement kernel; add
a habitat × movement interaction; discover why covariate resolution decides
whether any of this works; and fit all six animals.

**Time:** ~55 minutes. **Packages:** `amt`, `terra`, `survival`, `dplyr`,
`tidyr`, `lubridate`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

covs <- project(
  c(rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif"), rast("data/kruger_landcover.tif")),
  "EPSG:32736"
)
names(covs)
#> [1] "elevation" "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"    "cropland"
round(res(covs))
#> [1] 893 893
```
:::


::: {.callout-note}
Note the pixel size: **893 m**. Remember that number — it decides the outcome
of this entire exercise.
:::

## Task 1 — Build the strata


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
steps_for <- function(animal, rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(15)) {
  trk |>
    filter(id == animal) |>
    track_resample(rate = rate, tolerance = tolerance) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) |>
    steps_by_burst() |>
    filter(sl_ < 10000)          # drop the spatial outliers found in Class 3
}

set.seed(2026)
obs <- steps_for("Cilla")

ssf_dat <- obs |>
  random_steps(n_control = 15) |>
  extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")

c(strata = n_distinct(ssf_dat$step_id_), rows = nrow(ssf_dat))
#> strata   rows 
#>   3512  56192
names(ssf_dat)
#>  [1] "burst_"          "x1_"             "x2_"             "y1_"            
#>  [5] "y2_"             "sl_"             "ta_"             "t1_"            
#>  [9] "t2_"             "dt_"             "case_"           "step_id_"       
#> [13] "elevation_start" "trees_start"     "grassland_start" "shrubs_start"   
#> [17] "cropland_start"  "elevation_end"   "trees_end"       "grassland_end"  
#> [21] "shrubs_end"      "cropland_end"
```
:::


### Your turn

**1a.** Look inside a single stratum. What varies within it, and what does not?
**1b.** Why does `where = "both"` give you `_start` and `_end` columns?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ssf_dat |>
  filter(step_id_ == ssf_dat$step_id_[1]) |>
  transmute(case_, sl_ = round(sl_), ta_ = round(ta_, 2),
            elevation_start = round(elevation_start),
            elevation_end = round(elevation_end),
            grassland_end = round(grassland_end, 2)) |>
  head(16)
#> # A tibble: 16 × 6
#>    case_   sl_   ta_ elevation_start elevation_end grassland_end
#>  * <lgl> <dbl> <dbl>           <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
#>  1 TRUE    594  0.87             258           272          0.82
#>  2 FALSE    49 -1.11             258           258          0.92
#>  3 FALSE   487 -0.2              258           258          0.92
#>  4 FALSE   339 -0.32             258           258          0.92
#>  5 FALSE   287  0.78             258           270          0.87
#>  6 FALSE    55 -0.94             258           258          0.92
#>  7 FALSE   537  2.2              258           270          0.87
#>  8 FALSE   126 -2.85             258           258          0.92
#>  9 FALSE   246 -1.5              258           258          0.92
#> 10 FALSE     3  2.48             258           258          0.92
#> 11 FALSE   580 -0.16             258           258          0.92
#> 12 FALSE   147  0.85             258           258          0.92
#> 13 FALSE    35  0.49             258           258          0.92
#> 14 FALSE    20  0.98             258           258          0.92
#> 15 FALSE    83  1.87             258           270          0.87
#> 16 FALSE     6 -0.28             258           258          0.92
```
:::


Within a stratum: **one** row with `case_ = TRUE` (the step the animal took)
and 15 with `case_ = FALSE` (steps it could have taken). The start point, the
time, the animal and everything else about that moment are **identical** —
only the destination, and hence the `_end` covariates, vary.

That is the whole design. Because the likelihood compares only within strata,
every time-constant confounder cancels: hour of day, season, weather, the
animal's identity, its internal state. You get that control for free.

`where = "both"` extracts covariates at the start **and** end of each step.
You need both: `_end` covariates express **selection** (where did it go),
`_start` covariates modify the **movement kernel** (how does it move when
starting from here). Task 5 uses that distinction.
:::

## Task 2 — A basic SSF


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_ssf <- fit_issf(
  ssf_dat,
  case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end + strata(step_id_),
  model = TRUE
)

round(summary(m_ssf$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> elevation_end -0.0102    0.9899   0.0023 -4.5012   0.0000
#> grassland_end -0.0245    0.9758   0.2942 -0.0831   0.9338
```
:::


### Your turn

**2a.** Interpret the coefficients.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Coefficients are on the log scale, exactly as for an RSF, and there is no
intercept. `exp(coef)` is the **relative selection strength**: the factor by
which the relative probability of choosing a step multiplies per unit increase
in the covariate, compared with the other steps *available at that moment*.

Elevation is measured in metres, so its coefficient is per metre — small by
construction. Standardise if you want comparable effect sizes:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
zs <- ssf_dat |>
  mutate(across(c(elevation_end, grassland_end), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))))

m_z <- fit_issf(zs, case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end + strata(step_id_),
                model = TRUE)
round(summary(m_z$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> elevation_end -0.3189    0.7270   0.0708 -4.5012   0.0000
#> grassland_end -0.0033    0.9967   0.0403 -0.0831   0.9338
```
:::


Elevation is strongly and clearly negative. Grassland — the covariate that
mattered most in Class 7 — is indistinguishable from zero. Hold that thought.
:::

## Task 3 — A full iSSA

Add the movement terms so that the movement kernel is estimated jointly with
selection.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_issa <- fit_issf(
  ssf_dat,
  case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
          sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
          strata(step_id_),
  model = TRUE
)

round(summary(m_issa$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> elevation_end -0.0102    0.9898   0.0022 -4.5558   0.0000
#> grassland_end -0.0232    0.9770   0.2926 -0.0794   0.9367
#> sl_            0.0000    1.0000   0.0001  0.2731   0.7848
#> log(sl_)       0.0052    1.0052   0.0128  0.4037   0.6865
#> cos(ta_)       0.0058    1.0058   0.0269  0.2159   0.8291
```
:::


### Your turn

**3a.** Recover the realised movement kernel and compare it with the tentative one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tent_sl <- sl_distr(ssf_dat)
tent_ta <- ta_distr(ssf_dat)

upd_sl <- update_gamma(
  tent_sl,
  beta_sl     = coef(m_issa)[["sl_"]],
  beta_log_sl = coef(m_issa)[["log(sl_)"]]
)
upd_ta <- update_vonmises(tent_ta, beta_cos_ta = coef(m_issa)[["cos(ta_)"]])

data.frame(
  quantity = c("gamma shape", "gamma scale", "mean step (m)", "vonMises kappa"),
  tentative = round(c(tent_sl$params$shape, tent_sl$params$scale,
                      tent_sl$params$shape * tent_sl$params$scale,
                      tent_ta$params$kappa), 3),
  realised  = round(c(upd_sl$params$shape, upd_sl$params$scale,
                      upd_sl$params$shape * upd_sl$params$scale,
                      upd_ta$params$kappa), 3)
)
#>         quantity tentative realised
#> 1    gamma shape     0.607    0.612
#> 2    gamma scale   467.829  471.761
#> 3  mean step (m)   283.740  288.558
#> 4 vonMises kappa     0.717    0.723
```
:::


The **tentative** distribution is the one `random_steps()` fitted to the
observed steps and sampled the controls from. The **realised** kernel is what
the animal actually does once selection is accounted for.

Here they are almost identical, and the movement coefficients are
non-significant — meaning that for this animal, at this interval, habitat is
not detectably distorting the movement kernel.

::: {.callout-tip}
Do this arithmetic with `update_gamma()` / `update_vonmises()`, never by hand.
The relationship between the coefficients and the distribution parameters
depends on the parameterisation, and getting it wrong is easy and silent.
:::
:::

## Task 4 — Why grassland vanished

Class 7 found grassland to be the strongest covariate. Here it is nothing.
Something is wrong — and it is not the biology.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# How often does a control step land in the SAME raster cell as the start?
mean(ssf_dat$grassland_end == ssf_dat$grassland_start, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.6928025
median(obs$sl_)
#> [1] 150.1476
round(res(covs)[1])
#> [1] 893
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## The step is smaller than the pixel

The median hourly step is about 150 m. The land-cover cells are **893 m**
across. So roughly **69% of control steps land in the very same cell as the
step's origin** — the used step and its alternatives are assigned *identical*
covariate values, and the stratum contains no contrast for the model to
exploit.

An SSF can only detect selection for a covariate that **varies within the
animal's reach in one time step**. If your pixels are bigger than your steps,
you will find nothing, no matter how strong the real preference is.
:::

### Your turn

**4a.** Refit at 3- and 6-hourly intervals and watch the effect appear.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
compare_rates <- lapply(c(1, 3, 6), function(h) {
  o <- steps_for("Cilla", rate = hours(h), tolerance = minutes(15))
  set.seed(1)
  d <- o |> random_steps(n_control = 15) |> extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")
  f <- fit_issf(d, case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
                  sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_), model = TRUE)
  cc <- summary(f$model)$coefficients
  data.frame(
    interval_h  = h,
    strata      = n_distinct(d$step_id_),
    median_sl_m = round(median(o$sl_)),
    same_cell   = round(mean(d$grassland_end == d$grassland_start, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    grass_beta  = round(cc["grassland_end", "coef"], 3),
    grass_p     = round(cc["grassland_end", "Pr(>|z|)"], 4)
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

compare_rates
#>   interval_h strata median_sl_m same_cell grass_beta grass_p
#> 1          1   3512         150      0.69     -0.055  0.8535
#> 2          3   1172         478      0.43      0.220  0.5417
#> 3          6    584         934      0.21      0.648  0.1293
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(compare_rates$interval_h, compare_rates$same_cell, type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Sampling interval (h)", ylab = "Fraction of controls in the start cell",
     main = "Contrast available to the model")
plot(compare_rates$interval_h, compare_rates$grass_beta, type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "#c1440e", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Sampling interval (h)", ylab = "Grassland coefficient",
     main = "...and the effect it can detect")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=816}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


As the interval lengthens, steps get longer, controls reach further, fewer
land in the origin cell — and the grassland coefficient climbs from
essentially zero to a substantial positive value, recovering the selection
Class 7 detected.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not read this as "longer intervals are better"

You are trading one bias for another. Longer steps give more spatial contrast,
but they also **coarsen the behavioural question**: a 6-hour "step" is a
straight line drawn across six hours of real movement, and it no longer
represents a single movement decision.

The honest conclusion is that **893 m land cover is the wrong resolution for
hourly buffalo data**. The fix is finer covariates — Sentinel-2 at 10–20 m
would resolve this comfortably — not a coarser animal.

**The general rule:** your covariate resolution must be finer than your
typical step length, or the step selection design has nothing to compare.
:::
:::

## Task 5 — Habitat × movement interactions

Does the animal move *differently* depending on where it starts? Use the
6-hourly data, where there is contrast to work with.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
obs6 <- steps_for("Cilla", rate = hours(6), tolerance = minutes(30))
set.seed(7)
d6 <- obs6 |> random_steps(n_control = 20) |> extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")

m_int <- fit_issf(
  d6,
  case_ ~ grassland_end + elevation_end +
          sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
          sl_:grassland_start +
          cos(ta_):grassland_start +
          strata(step_id_),
  model = TRUE
)

round(summary(m_int$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                             coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> grassland_end             0.4761    1.6098   0.4244  1.1219   0.2619
#> elevation_end            -0.0145    0.9856   0.0033 -4.4284   0.0000
#> sl_                      -0.0006    0.9994   0.0003 -1.7349   0.0828
#> log(sl_)                 -0.0211    0.9791   0.0824 -0.2559   0.7980
#> cos(ta_)                 -1.9353    0.1444   0.4190 -4.6183   0.0000
#> sl_:grassland_start       0.0007    1.0007   0.0003  1.9028   0.0571
#> cos(ta_):grassland_start  2.2115    9.1297   0.4689  4.7169   0.0000
```
:::


### Your turn

**5a.** Interpret the two interaction terms.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The two interactions answer different questions from the selection terms:

- **`sl_:grassland_start`** — does the animal take **longer steps** when it
  starts in grassland? A positive coefficient means it moves *faster through*
  grassland; a negative one means it slows down and lingers, which is what you
  would expect where it feeds.
- **`cos(ta_):grassland_start`** — does it move **more directionally** from
  grassland? Positive means straighter paths; negative means more tortuous,
  the signature of area-restricted search.

Note carefully that these use `grassland_**start**`, the habitat at the
*origin* of the step. A common and serious error is to interact `sl_` with
`grassland_end`, which is not a movement statement at all — it conditions on
the destination and mangles the interpretation of both terms.

The combination is what makes iSSA worth the trouble: an RSF has no movement
component, so "goes there" and "behaves differently there" collapse into a
single undifferentiated measure of use.

### What these particular numbers say

Both interactions come out **positive**, and `cos(ta_)` has a large negative
main effect. Read them together:

- **Turning.** The main effect (`cos(ta_)` ≈ −1.9) applies where
  `grassland_start = 0`: away from grassland the animal's movement is strongly
  *anti-persistent* — it reverses direction, staying in a small area. Adding
  the interaction (≈ +2.2) gives roughly +0.3 in pure grassland: from
  grassland, movement is mildly **directional**.
- **Step length.** `sl_:grassland_start` is positive: steps starting in
  grassland are **longer**.

So at this six-hour scale the picture is the opposite of a foraging-patch
story: buffalo tend to move *into* grassland (`grassland_end` positive, though
imprecise) but cross it in long, straight steps, while their movement off
grassland is short and tortuous — consistent with grassland acting as a
travel matrix and the wooded/riverine areas as places to settle.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do not over-read this. `grassland_end` here is not statistically distinguishable
from zero for a single animal, and a six-hour step is a coarse summary of
movement. It is an interpretation to take to Task 6 and test across
individuals, not a conclusion.
:::
:::

## Task 6 — All six animals


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_animal <- function(animal) {
  o <- steps_for(animal, rate = hours(6), tolerance = minutes(30))
  if (nrow(o) < 100) return(NULL)
  set.seed(11)
  d <- o |> random_steps(n_control = 15) |> extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")
  f <- try(fit_issf(d, case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
                      sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_),
                    model = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(f, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  cc <- summary(f$model)$coefficients
  data.frame(id = animal, term = rownames(cc), beta = cc[, "coef"])
}

per_animal <- lapply(unique(trk$id), fit_animal) |> bind_rows()

per_animal |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = id, values_from = beta) |>
  mutate(across(-term, \(z) signif(z, 3)))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   term                Queen       Gabs      Cilla      Mvubu       Toni   Pepper
#>   <chr>               <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 elevation_end -0.00207    -0.0163    -0.0165    -0.0194    -0.00359   -1.63e-2
#> 2 grassland_end  1.01        0.158      0.65       0.308     -1.01       7.69e-1
#> 3 sl_            0.00000843  0.0000163 -0.0000142 -0.0000053 -0.0000297  4.54e-5
#> 4 log(sl_)      -0.0314      0.00911    0.0422     0.0328     0.0127     6.08e-3
#> 5 cos(ta_)       0.0129      0.00543    0.0231     0.00363   -0.00912   -1.15e-2
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
`sl_` is measured per **metre**, so its coefficient is tiny by construction and
rounds to zero at three decimals — `signif()` rather than `round()` keeps it
readable. This is a presentation problem, not a modelling one, but it is worth
handling before anyone concludes the effect is exactly zero.
:::

### Your turn

**6a.** Summarise across individuals. Which effects are consistent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pop <- per_animal |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(n_animals = n(),
            mean_beta = mean(beta),
            se = sd(beta) / sqrt(n()),
            t = mean_beta / se,
            p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = n() - 1),
            n_positive = sum(beta > 0),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_beta, se, t), \(z) round(z, 3)), p = round(p, 4))

pop
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   term          n_animals mean_beta    se      t      p n_positive
#>   <chr>             <int>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 cos(ta_)              6     0.004 0.005  0.763 0.480           4
#> 2 elevation_end         6    -0.012 0.003 -4.04  0.0099          0
#> 3 grassland_end         6     0.313 0.293  1.07  0.334           5
#> 4 log(sl_)              6     0.012 0.01   1.14  0.305           5
#> 5 sl_                   6     0     0      0.327 0.757           3
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
boxplot(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        las = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "Coefficient",
        main = "iSSA coefficients, 6 buffalo (6-hourly)")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
stripchart(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE,
           pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6), cex = 0.9)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=720}
:::
:::


Read the `n_positive` column alongside the p-value. With six animals, a term
with the same sign in 6 of 6 is strong evidence of a consistent
population-level effect even when the mean is imprecise; one that is positive
in 3 and negative in 3 is not a population effect however narrow its interval.

This two-stage summary is honest about sample size: your degrees of freedom
come from the number of **animals**, not the hundreds of thousands of rows in
the strata.

With more individuals you would move to a mixed conditional model —
`glmmTMB` with random slopes and the stratum-intercept variance fixed large,
following Muff et al. (2020).
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
*Suppose* an iSSA reported a positive coefficient on `grassland_end` and a
**negative** one on `sl_:grassland_start` (note: not the pattern our buffalo
showed). What would the animal be doing?

- [ ] Avoiding grassland but crossing it quickly
- [x] Moving into grassland, then slowing down once there
- [ ] Taking longer steps towards grassland
- [ ] The two results contradict each other

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Two different statements, and they fit together neatly.

`grassland_end` positive: among the steps available at each moment, the animal
**chooses** those ending in grassland — selection.

`sl_:grassland_start` negative: when it *starts* a step in grassland, that step
is **shorter** — it slows down.

Together: the animal heads into grassland and then lingers there. That is the
classic signature of a foraging patch, and it is exactly what a large grazer
should do.

An RSF cannot express this at all: it has no movement component, so "goes
there" and "slows down there" collapse into one undifferentiated measure of
use.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
You have Argos locations with 1–5 km error and a 30 m land-cover map. Should
you fit an iSSA?

- [ ] Yes — 30 m resolution gives excellent covariate contrast
- [x] No — the positional error is far larger than the covariate grain, so the covariate assigned to each step is essentially random
- [ ] Yes, but only with more control steps
- [ ] Yes, after projecting everything to UTM

::: {.quiz-feedback}
With kilometres of positional error, you do not know which 30 m cell the animal
was in — the land-cover value you extract is close to a random draw from a
large neighbourhood. Fine covariates cannot rescue coarse locations; they just
add noise with a confident-looking resolution.

This is the mirror image of Task 4. There the pixels were too **coarse**
relative to the steps; here they are too **fine** relative to the location
error. Both break the same requirement:

> the covariate must vary meaningfully **at the scale you can actually resolve
> the animal's position and movement**.

With Argos data, aggregate the covariates to something comparable to the error
(1–5 km), and ask a broader-scale question — an RSF at second order, not an
iSSA.
:::
:::
